His chief work, the three-volume Tribunal Sacramentale of 1642, set out moral theology plainly for confessors. He died at Ghent in 1661.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philosophy-of:
Immanuel Kant was the Königsberg philosopher whose critical system remade modern thought, born in 1724. He studied at his native university under Knutzen, learning Wolff's philosophy and Newton's physics, spent nine years tutoring after his father's death in 1746, and returned to Königsberg in 1755. Privatdozent until 1770, he held the philosophy chair until 1797 and died in 1804.

His pre-critical writings defended Wolff, but the Critique of Pure Reason of 1781 opened the critical period. It argues that mind shapes experience through its own forms, while soul, world, and God lie beyond proof as ideas of reason. The Critique of Practical Reason, the Critique of Judgment, and Religion within the Limits of Mere Reason followed, making morality, not dogma, religion's core. The entry judges the system agnostic in theology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-piedmont:
Piedmont was a region of northern Italy, its name from pedes montium, feet of the mountains, enclosed on three sides by the Alps. It holds the upper Po plain and Alpine valleys descending from the Pennine, Graian, Cottian, and Maritime ranges, bounded by Switzerland, France, Liguria, and Lombardy. Today it forms the provinces of Turin, Novara, Alessandria, and Cuneo.

Its passes to Gaul made it important from antiquity. Christianity, slow until the fourth century, spread fast in the fourth and fifth among a Romanized people, with early sees at Turin, Asti, and Aosta. Feudal marquessates of Ivrea, Susa, Saluzzo, and Montferrat divided it until Savoy's counts rose: Humbert I held Aosta, and his son Otto's marriage to Adelaide of Turin founded the later Piedmont. The survey follows Savoy to modern Italy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-charle:
Pierre Charles L'Enfant was the French-born engineer who planned Washington, born in France in August 1755. Trained as an engineer, he joined Lafayette as a volunteer for the revolted colonists in 1777. He became captain of engineers in 1778 and brevet major in 1783, serving valiantly through the Revolutionary War. Afterwards he remodelled New York's old City Hall for the First Congress.

When the federal city's site was chosen, he spent much of 1791 on his Plan of the City, intended for the Permanent Seat of Government on the Potomac. A quick temper and overbearing disposition brought quarrels with superiors, and Washington dismissed him on 1 March 1792 before his plan was carried out. He refused payment for the Capitol plan and a West Point professorship, built Washington fortifications in 1812, quarrelled again, and sought recompense from Congress in vain. He died near Bladensburg in 1825, poor and forgotten.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-cousta:
Pierre Coustant was a learned Maurist Benedictine, born at Compiègne on 30 April 1654. Schooled by Jesuits there, he entered Saint-Rémi at Reims at seventeen, took vows in 1672, and studied under François Lamy at Soissons. In 1681 his superiors sent him to Saint-Germain-des-Prés to help edit St. Augustine, separating genuine writings from spurious ones.

His learning won him the new edition of St. Hilary of Poitiers, replacing Erasmus's defective 1523 text, and work on the Maurist Breviary and Augustine's general index. Immediately after Augustine's works appeared in 1700, he undertook a complete collection of papal letters from Clement I to Innocent III, sifting authentic from false and restoring texts chronologically. After more than twenty years he published the first volume in 1721, covering 67 to 440, with a 150-page preface on papal primacy. He died that same year at Saint-Germain-des-Prés.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-olivai:
Pierre Olivaint was a French Jesuit priest whose path from unbelief to faith made him a symbol of Catholic revival in France. He was born in Paris in 1816 to parents without religion. He absorbed Voltaire's ideas at school, yet by 1837, moved by Lacordaire's preaching, he professed the faith to Father Ravignan.

At the Normal School he gathered a circle of Catholic students known for prayer and charity. He taught history and in 1845 entered the Jesuit novitiate at Laval on the very day of a parliamentary attack on the order. He worked with the Conferences of Saint Vincent de Paul. In 1871, during the Paris Commune, he was seized and shot with fellow prisoners in the Rue Haxo.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-plain-chant:
Plain chant is the unaccompanied church music of the early Middle Ages, the Church's own music before polyphony, singing in many parts, appeared. Growing up gradually in worship, it remained the sole music of the Church until the ninth century. It then held a place of honour beside the new music and served as the foundation on which polyphony was built.

The name cantus planus, plain song, arose among theorists of the twelfth or thirteenth century to set it against measured music, with notes of strict relative length. Also called Gregorian chant after Saint Gregory I and Roman chant for its Roman form, it faded in esteem after the sixteenth century. Yet the Church always kept it as her proper music, and the entry traces its revival in modern times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-postulant:
Postulancy is the trial stage ere the novitiate, in place since monastic life began. In the East, the would-be monk met many rebuffs, to test whether his call was true. The custom passed to the West. Benedict's rule bids the house not take a newcomer too lightly, but try the spirits. If, after he repeats his plea, he bears rebuffs and blocks for four or five days and still holds on, the door opens to him.

In varied orders the trial ran from three to ten days. Then came a novitiate of one, two, or three years, once seen as training, not as its first stage. After taking him in, houses of old sent the man back to the world on open leave, free to come back when he chose. The Customs of St Victor notes the practice as common to many houses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-principality-:
Waldeck-Pyrmont was a former state of the German Empire, covering 433 square miles. It held two parts. South Waldeck, ringed by Prussian Hesse-Nassau and Westphalia, held 407 square miles and 49,965 folk in 1905. North Pyrmont, ringed by Lippe, Brunswick, and Hanover, held 26 square miles and 9,162 folk. In 1905 it counted 56,341 Protestants, 1,890 Catholics, and 629 Jews. The land takes its name from Waldeck castle on the Eider, a west Fulda branch.

About 1150 Widukind V of Schwalenberg seized the castle and styled himself Count of Waldeck. Waldeck stood as a Hessian fief from 1438, a tie ended in 1846. In 1631, when Gleichen's counts died out, Waldeck gained Pyrmont. In the war of 1866 Waldeck backed Prussia and joined the North German Confederation. Prussia took over the administration by the Treaty of Accession of 1867.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-redemption-in:
Redemption means either strict deliverance for a price or ransom paid, or simple deliverance by power from oppression, violence or captivity. This encyclopedia entry traces the idea in Hebrew through the verbs ga'al and padah, with kopher, ransom, closely related. Ga'al serves technically in the Mosaic Law for redeeming an inheritance, a vowed thing or tithes by price. Padah serves for redeeming the first-born of children or animals.

Outside the Law, and in relation to Israel's God, both verbs mean simple salvation or deliverance by power. The New Testament narrows redemption to man's rescue from sin by Christ's death, expressed by lutroumai, from lutron, a ransom, and its derivatives. The entry thus moves from law-court prices in ancient Israel to the theological heart of the New Testament, with Schurér, Nowack and Schwalm among its scholarly sources on Jewish life and law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-remiremont:
Remiremont in the Vosges is a monastery and nunnery under the Rule of Saint Benedict. Saints Romaricus and Amatus founded it in 620 on hills above the present town, whence its name, Romarici Mons. The monastery later became a priory of the Canons Regular of Saint Augustine, who gave it in 1623 to the Benedictines of the Congregation of Saint Vannes. In 1768 it held ten monks and a revenue of fifty-five hundred livres.

For three centuries the nunnery stood beside the monastery. In 910, as the Huns wasted the country, the nuns built a fortified convent in the valley with Emperor Louis the Third's help. The town of Remiremont grew around that convent, the relics of Romaricus and Amatus were moved there from the monastery, and Leo the Ninth enriched it with many more relics. Fire destroyed the convent in 1057 and scattered the nuns.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reservation-o:
Reservation of the Blessed Sacrament is the keeping, after the Liturgy, of part of the consecrated elements for the Communion of the sick or other pious purposes. Its extreme antiquity is beyond dispute. Justin Martyr's first detailed account of Eucharistic practice already sends a portion by deacons to the absent. Irenaeus records presbyters sending the Eucharist between districts, and Tertullian uses the very word reservare.

The entry draws a firm line about later practice. No reliable evidence shows the Sacrament kept in churches before the year 1000, or even later, so that the faithful might visit it or pray before it. Evidence cited for such a custom tells the other way on inspection. Even Optatus's phrase for the altar, throne of the Body and Blood of Christ, is read by the entry as telling the other way.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sacra-jam-spl:
Sacra jam splendent are the opening words of the Matins hymn for the Feast of the Holy Family. The Holy See set up the feast in 1893 as a greater double, placing it on the third Sunday after Epiphany. Leo XIII composed the three hymns of the Breviary Office, for Vespers, Matins, and Lauds. The Matins hymn has nine Sapphic stanzas of classical type. Its first stanza pictures a thousand lights on garlanded shrines and altars.

The Vespers and Lauds hymns are in classical dimeter iambics, four-lined stanzas, six and seven respectively, besides the usual Marian doxology. All three hymns overflow with spiritual warmth, graceful phrasing, and classical dignity of form. They reflect the pope's sentiment in his letter establishing a Pious Association for the Holy Family and in his encyclical on working-men's condition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sebastian-bra:
Sebastian Brant, German humanist and poet, was born at Strasbourg in 1457 or 1458 and died there in 1521. At Basel university he first studied philosophy, then turned to law, taking his doctorate in canon and civil law in 1489, while lecturing from 1484 and practising at the same time. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a patriot poet of empire and Church.

His Latin and German poems set out religious and political ideals. Maximilian's election as emperor filled Brant and many patriots with hope: emperor as supreme temporal ruler of Christian nations, Church as supreme spiritual ruler, was his great desire, colouring all his verse. He hoped above all for restored imperial power in Germany, but disappointment followed. In 1499 Basel left the empire for the Swiss confederacy, and Brant's position there grew untenable.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-servants-of-t:
The Servants of the Most Blessed Sacrament, an order of nuns, was founded in 1858 by Pierre-Julien Eymard. Mother Margaret of the Blessed Sacrament helped him. The Archbishop of Paris authorized the work. Pius IX erected it canonically in 1871, and Leo XIII approved its constitutions in 1885. Its aim is solemn and perpetual adoration of Christ in the Sacrament of the Altar, offered above all else for the love of men.

Each sister makes three adorations in twenty-four hours, two by day and one by night, and the Divine Office is said in choir. The community is contemplative and cloistered, with its mother-house at Angers. Houses followed at Lyons in 1874, Paris in 1876, and Binche in Belgium in 1894, and a Canadian foundation later gained its own novitiate. The entry counts thirteen perpetually professed sisters and fifteen novices.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-siger-of-brab:
Siger of Brabant stands as the undisputed leader of Latin Averroism in the 1260s and 1270s. Many arts masters took up his principles, and Dante immortalized him in the Paradiso as the light of Siger who syllogized unwelcome truths. His illustrious colleague Saint Thomas Aquinas expressly refuted his teachings. Few solid details of his life survive.

A master of arts at Paris, he led university agitations for ten years, working with the legate Simon de Brie on discipline. From 1272 to 1275 he held the university rector Alberic of Reims in check, heading an opposition drawn from the Garlande quarter. Condemned in 1270, he kept teaching, and a second condemnation in 1277 ended his career. Hauled before France's Grand Inquisitor and condemned, he appealed to Rome and died at Orvieto between 1281 and 1284, murdered by his secretary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-william-d:
William D'Avenant, poet and dramatist born at Oxford in February 1606, died in London on 7 April 1668. Second son of John D'Avenant, vintner and owner of the Crown Tavern inn where Shakespeare often stayed. He may have been the poet's godson, though the tale making him Shakespeare's natural son lacks foundation. Schooled at Oxford, he became page to Frances, Duchess of Richmond, then entered the service of Fulke Greville, Lord Brooke.

He began writing plays in 1628 and ten years later succeeded Ben Jonson as Poet Laureate. Warmly royalist in the Civil War, he was knighted by Charles I in 1643. After the king's defeat he fled to France in 1644 and became a Catholic. He served Queen Henrietta Maria's correspondence with the king, and faced imprisonment and danger to his life before release in 1651. In 1656 he helped revive English stage performances, silent since 1641, and after the Restoration Charles II patronized his writing and productions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ethelbert-:
Ethelbert, king of Kent from 560 to 616, opened England to the Roman mission by welcoming Augustine with fair dealing. Son of Eormenric and descendant of Hengest, he failed to wrest Britain's overlordship from Ceawlin of Wessex, but his marriage to Bertha, daughter of the Frankish king Charibert, raised his standing. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 24 February 616.

Though himself a worshipper of Odin, he gave Bertha the old Roman church of St. Martin at Canterbury and full freedom for her faith. When Augustine landed in 597, Ethelbert met him with hospitality, caution, and a noble sense of fair play. The entry shows a pagan king whose tolerance prepared the ground for conversion, both his people's and, in time, his own.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-vigilius-b:
Vigilius, bishop of Trent and martyr, converted Arians and idolaters across the Tyrol. Born about 353, his father is unknown, though some name Theodosius. His mother Maxentia and brothers Claudian and Magorian are all counted saints. Brought young to Trent, he studied at Athens, winning fame for sanctity and learning, and there befriended John Chrysostom.

Returning through Rome in 380, the people of Trent chose him bishop by acclamation, and Valerian of Aquileia, or possibly Ambrose of Milan, consecrated him. Ambrose urged him to oppose marriages with heathens. Vigilius laboured to convert Trent's Arians and the idolaters of his diocese, preaching beyond it into Brescia and Verona. Stoned by pagans at Val Rendena, he died on 26 June 405, patron of Trent and Tyrol.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-vincent:
Vincent of Saragossa, deacon and martyr under Diocletian in 304, stands as Spain's most renowned martyr. He is named in the Roman Martyrology for 22 January, pictured in a deacon's dalmatic with a cross, a raven, a grate, or a fire-pile as emblems. Valencia, Saragossa, and Portugal honour him as patron, and vintners, brickmakers, and sailors invoke him.

Born at Saragossa to Eutricius and Enola of Osca, he studied under Bishop Valerius, who had an impediment of speech and charged Vincent with preaching in the diocese. Governor Dacian dragged bishop and deacon to Valencia, where Vincent endured torture and death. Augustine testifies that his Acts were read in African churches by the late fourth century, though the present Acts date from the eighth or ninth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-blessed-e:
Christ's presence under bread and wine gives this long doctrinal entry its starting point: the Blessed Eucharist counts unquestionably as a sacrament of the Church. It fits the classic definition, an outward sign of inward grace instituted by Christ. Yet its precise nature has taxed theologians, since Protestants do not deny the rite's existence while disputing its meaning.

Neither consecration alone nor communion alone makes the sacrament, the entry argues. Consecration is the sacrificial act, communion the reception. Most theologians locate the sacrament in the union of both factors: the Eucharistic species together with the Body and Blood hidden beneath them. Matter, form, minister, effects, and necessity are then examined in a full scholastic survey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-count-of-:
Flemish noble Lamoral, Count of Egmont, beheaded at Brussels on 5 June 1568, is the tragic figure of this entry. Born at La Hamaide in Hainault on 18 November 1522, he was heir to one of the Low Countries' oldest houses. He went to Spain in 1538 with elder brother Charles and fought at Algiers in 1541, where Charles was hurt and died the next year. Lamoral took title and estates.

Wedding Sabina of Bavaria in 1544, with emperor and King of the Romans present, he won campaigns under Charles V. At twenty-six Charles gave him the Golden Fleece and confidential missions, including seeking Queen Mary's hand in England. Loyalty to Spain and to Netherlandish liberties at once doomed him when Alba's regime struck, and his scaffold death made him a martyr of freedom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-establish:
Union of Church and State, called establishment, is the relation defined in this short entry for Catholic and Protestant lands alike, despite deep differences of principle. The Establishment, or Established Church, names above all the system set up by law in Scotland, in Ireland until 1869, and especially in England. Pre-Reformation England's church was the people's religion, established by the people's spontaneous act.

Post-Reformation church, by contrast, came imposed by legal enactment on royal supremacy's principle. Papal jurisdiction passed entire to the Crown, not merely swept away. Except brief Catholic return under Mary, 1553 to 1558, and Commonwealth years, 1649 to 1660, those arrangements have ever since limited the Church's freedom of action in England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-society-o:
Priests devoted wholly to worship of the Holy Eucharist form the congregation founded here in story. Pierre-Julien Eymard launched it in Paris on 1 June 1856, aiming at a society given exclusively to Eucharistic worship. Pius IX approved it by briefs of 1856 and 1858, and by decree of 3 June 1863 approved its rule for ten years, with perpetual approval from Leo XIII in 1895.

Père de Cuers first joined the founder, then Père Champion, and the community thrived. A novitiate opened in 1862 for priests and lay brothers: priests recite the Office in choir, brothers share perpetual adoration and household work. Blessed Sacrament exposed always, adorers never absent, hourly prayer at the bell's signal mark its life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-grant:
Thomas Grant, first Bishop of Southwark, was born at Ligny-les-Aires, France, in 1816 to Irish parents and died at Rome in 1870. His father, an Irish soldier who rose from sergeant to a commission, sent him to Ushaw in 1829 and then to the English College at Rome, where he was ordained in 1841. At twenty-eight he became rector of the English College and agent for the English bishops.

Grant did much of the quiet work behind the restoration of the English hierarchy, translating documents for Propaganda and drafting the historical preface to the decree of 1850. Consecrated Bishop of Southwark in July 1851, he won trust quickly, negotiating with the government for military, naval and prison chaplains where Cardinal Wiseman could not deal directly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-trent:
A diocese, suffragan of Salzburg, made famous across the world by the general council held there from 1545 to 1563. Its territory came under Rome in 15 B.C., and Abundantius appears as Bishop of Trent at Aquileia in 381, while St. Vigilius, stoned to death before forty, guarded the gospel seed in the region.

Set between Germany and Italy, Trent felt both influences, staying under Aquileia until 1751 and becoming an independent ecclesiastical principality under Bishop Ulrich II. That independence ended in 1803, and Bishop Emmanuel Maria of Thun, expelled in 1807 for refusing Bavarian demands on his clergy, returned only after the Tyrolese freed themselves.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-richard-s:
Richard Sergeant was an English martyr executed at Tyburn on 20 April 1586. Probably a younger son of Thomas Sergeant of Stone in Gloucestershire by Katherine Tyre of Hardwick, he took his degree at Oxford in February 1570-71. He reached the English College at Reims on 25 July 1581. Ordained subdeacon at Reims in April 1582, deacon at Soissons in June 1582, and priest at Laon in April 1583, he said his first Mass on 21 April.

He left for England on 10 September and was indicted at the Old Bailey on 17 April 1586 as Richard Lea alias Longe. With him was condemned and suffered William Thomson, a native of Blackburn in Lancashire. Thomson had reached the English College at Reims on 28 May 1583 and was ordained priest in Reims cathedral in March 1583-84. Thomson was arrested in the house of Roger Line.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-thurston-:
Thurston Hunt was a Yorkshire martyr executed at Lancaster in March 1601. A member of the Carlton Hall family near Leeds, he had studied at Reims in 1583 and 1584. His fellow sufferer, Robert Middleton, nephew of Margaret Clitheroe, had studied at Reims and Rome. In November 1600 Middleton was arrested by chance near Preston.

Hunt joined three other Catholics in a failed rescue attempt and was captured after a long struggle. Both men were heavily ironed day and night and, feet tied beneath their horses' bellies, were paraded in disgrace to London and back to Lancaster. Condemned for their priesthood, they were executed there. No one would hire out a horse to drag them to the gallows, and their relics were eagerly carried off afterward.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vermont:
Vermont is surveyed as a New England state, 10,212 square miles, bounded by Massachusetts, New Hampshire across the Connecticut River, New York across Lake Champlain, and Quebec in Canada. The Green Mountains, which give the state its name, run its full length, with five peaks over 4,000 feet. Mount Mansfield highest at 4,389 feet, and slopes thick with spruce and other evergreens.

Its Catholic story begins with Samuel Champlain, the Catholic nobleman who named the region. The little chapel at Fort Anne in 1666, where the first Mass within the present state was offered. From that first sacred building the entry follows missions, parishes, and the growth of the Church in a state of scattered farms, forests. Lake traffic by way of the Champlain Canal to the Hudson.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vexilla-regis:
Vexilla Regis Prodeunt, the banners of the king advance, is a world-famous hymn by Venantius Fortunatus, first sung in procession on 19 November 569 when a relic of the True Cross. Sent by Emperor Justin II at St Radegund's request, was carried in great pomp from Tours to her monastery of the Holy Cross at Poitiers.

Its original processional use survives in the Roman Missal on Good Friday. The Blessed Sacrament moves from the repository to the high altar. Its principal home is the Divine Office: the Breviary assigns it to Vespers from the Saturday before Passion Sunday through Maundy Thursday, and to feasts of the Holy Cross. Originally eight stanzas, it lost stanzas in the tenth century and again under Urban VIII's revisers, who reshaped it for classical metre.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-visits-to-the:
Visits to the Blessed Sacrament are a comparatively modern devotion. In it Christ's presence in the Eucharist is honoured with the ceremonial due to a sovereign dwelling in a place of his dominions. In the tabernacle, the image runs, Christ holds court and grants audience to all who draw near. The practice depends entirely on ceremonial reservation of the sacrament.

Attempts to prove an early Church custom of special external veneration for the reserved species when carried to the sick break down on closer investigation, the entry argues. Even today, it notes, the Greek Church knows no genuflection to the Blessed Sacrament, though it treats the sacrament respectfully, and the devotion's history is traced as a western development.
colonel-starbottle-s-client:
Bret Harte leads this collection with the longest of its nine California tales. Colonel Starbottle, the roaring Democratic orator of Calaveras, returns to his law practice between campaigns, shotgun by his chair. A stranger walks into his Rough and Ready office on a blistering day with a case that draws out the Colonel's chivalry and his bluster alike.

The other pieces range across Harte's mining-country cast. A postmistress at Laurel Run, a night at Hays, a new assistant at the Pine Clearing school, and a treasure from a Spanish galleon each get a story. One tale is frankly ghostly, at Stukeley Castle. Together they show Harte's standard mix of sentiment, comedy, and rough justice in the diggings.
complete-original-short-stories-of-guy-d:
Guy de Maupassant's short stories are gathered here entire, in the English translation credited on the title page to Albert M. C. McMaster, A. E. Henderson, Mme. Quesada, and others. The contents are arranged volume by volume. Boule de Suif, the story that made his name in 1880, stands first in the first volume, ahead of Two Friends and Father Milon.

The range across the volumes is the whole of his world. War stories of the Prussian occupation stand beside peasant tales of Normandy, Parisian adultery, and studies of madness and greed. The Story of a Farm Girl, Mother Sauvage, Miss Harriet, and Mademoiselle Fifi mark the heights. Maupassant wrote some three hundred stories in ten years; this set aims to hold them all between its covers.
considerations-on-representative-governm:
Considerations on Representative Government, by John Stuart Mill, sets out Mill's case for how a free people should be governed. Mill admits in his preface that the principles are ones he had worked toward for most of his life. The novelty, he says, lies in bringing them together and showing their connection, at a moment when debates on reform of Parliament had shaken both parties' faith in their old creeds.

Opening chapters ask how far a people chooses its own form of government, and what makes one form good. Mill's answer joins two tests: a government should improve the people's character and manage their affairs well. From there he weighs voting, representation of minorities, and the dangers of an all powerful assembly. The book became a founding text for modern arguments about democracy, competence, and who should hold a share of power.

donal-grant:
George MacDonald sent his shepherd-scholar Donal Grant down from a Scottish hillside in this long Highland novel, told partly in broad Scots with a glossary at the back. Donal, a poor, devout young man, walks out to seek work and becomes tutor at a castle ruled by the Earl of Morven. Lady Arctura, the earl's niece, and a house full of secrets wait for him there: lost rooms, a crypt, a hidden will.

MacDonald mixes romance with theology, giving Donal long talks on death, communism, and the soul between the Gothic turns. Ghosts, a housekeeper's plots, and a diseased conscience fill the eighty-four chapters. It is MacDonald at full stretch, part fairy tale for grown-ups, part sermon with a plot.
due-south-or-cuba-past-and-present: Due South, or Cuba Past and Present. The Cuban survey. This book preserves that travelogue. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
egmont:
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe's Egmont, translated by Anna Swanwick, dramatizes the Dutch revolt against Spain in five acts. The introductory note dates the writing: begun in 1775 when Goethe was twenty-six, finished at Rome in 1787 after twelve years of intervals. Count Egmont, beloved and careless, trusts his popularity against the Duke of Alva's rigor.

Clara, the burgher girl who loves him, treasures a keepsake she did not win by diligence and toil yet wears next her heart. Egmont jests about selling his horse to Alva's son Ferdinand in the very scene of his arrest. Beethoven's music later fixed the play's fame. Goethe makes Egmont's openness both his glory and his doom.
einhard-life-charlemagne-grant:
Einhard, a courtier and friend of Charlemagne, wrote his Life of the emperor around 830, soon after Charlemagne's death. A. J. Grant's 1905 translation, from his Early Lives of Charlemagne, is the text here, complete with prologue, all 33 chapters, and the emperor's will. Einhard modeled his work on Suetonius's lives of the Roman emperors.

He covers the wars that built the empire, the government of the court, and Charlemagne's private habits: his dress, his meals, his love of swimming and of books read aloud. The portrait is warm but not blind. No medieval biography is closer to its subject. The will, dividing his treasure among churches, closes the book.
galusha-the-magnificent:
Joseph C. Lincoln's Galusha the Magnificent opens on a foggy Cape Cod road in October. Horatio Pulcifer, a political fixer of East Wellmouth, drives his flivver home in serene self-satisfaction. Rain drips, the foghorn groans, and Pulcifer sings a music-hall tune. Into his scheming world comes his cousin Galusha Bancroft.

Galusha is a shy, absent-minded Egyptologist, rich, unworldly, and magnificent only in his oblivion. A bank failure, a haunted house, and a stock swindle test the village around him. Martha Phipps, the capable housekeeper, manages what Galusha cannot. Lincoln writes his Cape in dialect and affection, letting grafters collide with innocence. The joke of the title turns tender: the magnificent man is the one who never thinks of himself. Few American regional novels are cosier or better humoured.
govdocs-archive_org-leroy-cool-meets-the:
Alexander Baron, a British writer and debunker, wrote Leroy Cool Meets the 9/11 Truth Movement as a satirical dialogue. His fictional character Leroy Cool takes on proponents of conspiracy theories about the September 11 attacks.

The piece is staged as a debate, with Cool pressing the truthers on their claims about controlled demolition, government plots, and the rest of the movement's case. Baron writes to mock rather than to investigate, and his polemical comedy is pointed and sharp. It survives as a sample of the backlash literature that grew up against the 9/11 truth movement.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AmericansforEff:
Americans for Effective Law Enforcement was an organization that backed police and prosecutors in the court fights of the Vietnam era. This news article covers its move to argue before the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit.

The group sought to support upholding the contempt convictions arising from the Chicago Seven trial, the stormy case against antiwar protesters charged after the 1968 Democratic convention. Law-and-order groups like this one tried to weigh in on the prosecution's side of that fight. The clipping preserves a small move in the long legal war over the Chicago trials and their aftermath.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIALawrenceVint:
Vint Lawrence helped run the CIA's secret war in Laos between 1962 and 1966, one of the agency's young officers in the mountains. Then he became a political illustrator in Washington, and Connecticut Walker's profile, From the CIA to the Drawing Board, follows that unlikely second act.

Lawrence's drawings appeared in the capital's papers and journals, signed work where his agency years had been anonymous. The profile dwells on the trade: covert operations exchanged for caricature, Laos for the drawing board. It is a career-change story with few parallels, preserved from the magazine press of the capital.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CranorMillicent:
Milicent Cranor wrote a report titled Head Wound about the medical evidence in President Kennedy's killing. Rather than argue one theory, the report gathers a constellation of statements about the president's head wound. It also introduces a longer study of the medical testimony on the head injuries.

Cranor's approach is to set the statements side by side so readers can see where witnesses and doctors agree or conflict. The head wound has always been the most disputed part of the medical record. Her report serves as a guide into that dispute, organizing who said what before the deeper study begins.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-StoneWClement_S: Maxine Cheshire's VIP column in the Washington Post tracked the social and political gossip of the capital. The January 1974 clippings gathered here cover Spiro Agnew's house sale, businessman W. Clement Stone, and E. Howard Hunt of Watergate fame. Read together, they show what Washington readers were told about the powerful in the months when the Nixon White House was falling apart.
